findings.text: Within the first paragraph a newcomer learns what Athena is, who it is for and what problem it solves. That answers "what is it" and "why it matters" right away.
findings.source: header lede: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable."

findings.text: What to do next is linked from the top. The steps are concrete: prerequisites, clone, setup, and an example command (`athena ask "add a changelog"`). So a newcomer can act.
findings.source: header: "Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself" and the Next steps section: "Before installing, have git 2.40 or later, a C linker, curl, and either Claude Code or npm"

findings.text: There is no step to change into the cloned folder (for example `cd athena`) between cloning and running ./setup.sh. A first-time user who pastes the commands in order will see setup.sh fail.
findings.source: Next steps: "Get the code: git clone https://github.com/doodla/athena.git" then "Install Athena from the checkout: ./setup.sh"

findings.text: Someone who arrives at Athena's site finds almost all of the page is a detailed study of a different tool, firstmate, with 12 transition cards and 45 claims. After three paragraphs, the page has little more to say about Athena. A newcomer may not see why they should read this much detail about firstmate.
findings.source: Title: "Athena explains how firstmate handles work"; sections States, Counters, Transitions, Claims and sources

findings.text: This link is in the public header but speaks to an owner. A newcomer will not know if it applies to them or what the proposals are.
findings.source: header: "Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision."

findings.text: The walkthrough uses "unheld", "open captain call" and "merge authority", but neither the "Words used first" list nor the Glossary defines them. That leaves gaps in a section that is otherwise defined with care.
findings.source: Start here, step 1: "A spawn is accepted only for an unheld, unblocked item."; step 7: "still an open captain call"

findings.text: Each state appears only as a name, a tag and claim links, with no one-line description. A reader has to go to the Glossary to learn what each state means.
findings.source: States of a piece of work: "ready waiting"

findings.text: The same facts are repeated many times: definitions in two places, and the yolo/red/capacity rules in the walkthrough, the failure list, the cards and the Glossary. This makes the page longer than a newcomer needs, though it does keep each section readable on its own.
findings.source: "Words used first" leadin: "Each is defined here, and again in the Glossary at the end of the page."

findings.text: The page says plainly that nothing was run and every claim comes from reading the source. A newcomer can see how far to trust the study.
findings.source: Limits of this study, f1: "no failure or retry edge was observed; every claim is marked read."

findings.text: This section doesn't say which repository holds the studies/ folder, so a newcomer can't find the source data.
findings.source: About this page: "the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data this page is generated from."
